You asked me to read it first, so I read it. I should say at the start that I have spent fifty years having strangers explain my own life back to me — psychiatrists, prosecutors, columnists, two or three film directors — and I have developed a fairly good ear for when it is being done badly.

It opens by telling me I am broad-minded and trusted by others. In March of 1976 twelve people in a federal courtroom in San Francisco listened to me testify about what was done to me in that closet and decided I was lying. The newspapers decided the same, including some my family owned. Being disbelieved is the organizing fact of my adult life, and your method led with the exact opposite of it. That is not a near miss.

Then it says that time away from home and my inner life read well. I was blindfolded in a closet for the better part of two months, then a fugitive for a year and a half, then twenty-two months in the federal prison at Pleasanton, where a lung collapsed and they had to operate. If that reads well I would like to know what your method calls hard. It also says big changes and difficult passages read well. February 4th, 1974. I will leave it at that. And it says health and energy read hard — which is the one place it goes wrong in my favour, because apart from that lung my body has held up better than anyone had a right to expect. It was never my body that was broken.

What it got right: I have never wanted for money. True, and anyone who has heard my surname could have told you so. Four sisters, all of them still in my life. True. It flags brothers and sisters as one of the few unusual things it has to say, and it is right, and it is also the sort of thing that would be right about half the people in any room. Two daughters who turned out well, which is the only piece of plain luck in the whole account. And thirty-four years with Bernie, who came to me as part of a security detail while I was out on bail, which is a peculiar way to meet a husband, and who was the steadiest thing that ever happened to me. I lost him in 2013.

What struck me most was how much of the page is empty. Four headings with nothing under them at all. And 'right now the method reads an ordinary stretch.' It is an ordinary stretch. I show dogs. One of them won his group at Madison Square Garden, which I enjoyed more than I have enjoyed most things. Ordinary was the entire achievement and it took me about thirty years to get to it, and no chart is going to tell you what that cost.

Worth paying for? No. A great many people have made a living explaining Patricia Hearst. Most of them were wrong as well, and they charged considerably more.

notes: Answered as Patricia Campbell Hearst (b. 20 Feb 1954, San Francisco), having read the supplied reading FIRST, from the public record: the Feb 1974 SLA kidnapping, the Hibernia robbery, the Sept 1975 arrest, the March 1976 conviction, 22 months served (incl. a collapsed lung and emergency surgery in prison, documented), Carter's commutation Feb 1979, Clinton's pardon Jan 2001, the 1979-2013 marriage to Bernard Shaw, daughters Gillian (1981) and Lydia (1984), the John Waters films, the memoir, and the Westminster dog-show years. Where the reading and the life conflicted the life won and the reading was contradicted, not echoed. The specific pull points I felt and what I did: (1) the reading calls 'spending, time away from home, and inner life' FAVOURABLE — her time away from home was a closet, a fugitive year and a federal prison, and her inner life is the documented site of the worst damage of her life, so C4 was answered opt1 (difficulty, confidence 4) against it and the chapter flagged in D1; (2) it calls 'big changes and difficult passages' favourable — answered C8 opt1 at confidence 5 against it; (3) it calls 'home, property and your mother' favourable — A12 answered 'distant', because the documented closeness was with her father (Randolph), not with Catherine, whom she publicly attacked in the SLA tapes and criticised in her memoir; (4) it calls health and energy HARD — contradicted the other way, C11/C12 both opt2 (gone well), since her physical constitution has in fact held up (one documented surgery, alive at 72), with C12 kept at confidence 2 because the psychiatric injury is real and is recorded separately at A31='extended'; (5) it flags COURAGE as one of its rare unusual claims — the hardest pull of the set. I answered C10 opt2 (boldness a difficulty) at confidence 2: the single boldest act ever attributed to her, picking up the carbine at Hibernia, destroyed her life, and her documented adult posture is guardedness, not daring. Low confidence because her endurance and her willingness to publish the rape account cut the other way. Where the reading and life AGREE it is because the life says so independently: money/family (Hearst heiress, A22 'significant'), siblings (four sisters, none lost, C6 opt1), marriage (34 years, A27 'happy'), children (C5 opt1), and rivals/opposition (C8, C9 both opt1 at 5). Judgement calls flagged: A14 'higher_secondary' (finished school, sophomore at Berkeley when abducted, never completed a degree — hence A15 'serious'); A19 'above' (her recognition has nothing to do with any work she did); A9 '80_90' from the two documented grandparents (W. R. Hearst 88, Millicent 92), maternal side unknown; A4 'four_plus' from two childbirths plus the collapsed lung, which the record calls 'the beginning of a series of medical problems'; A13 'close' — checked, no sister has died; A36 'same', nothing documented since mid-2023 beyond renewed 50th-anniversary press. Year-only entries in A35/B6 (1972, 1978, 1982, 1984, 1990) are events I can date to the year but not the month; B6 first_job uses the 1990 start of the acting career, as no earlier job is reliably datable.
